Spiritual Franciscans
SPIR-i-choo-uhl fran-SIS-kuhnz
noun
The rigorist wing of the Franciscan order in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries; from Francis of Assisi and the Latin spiritualis.

📖 Biblical Definition

The Spiritual Franciscans were the rigorist party within the Franciscan order who, in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, insisted on the strictest observance of Francis’s rule of absolute poverty against the laxer Conventual majority, and who came to be entangled with the apocalyptic prophecies of Joachim of Fiore. The dictionary grants what is honorable: a protest against the wealth and worldliness of the church, a desire to follow Christ in plainness and contentment, and a witness against the corruption of a hierarchy grown rich. Scripture does commend contentment—having food and raiment, let us be therewith content—and warns that no man can serve God and mammon. Yet the movement fell into two errors the dictionary must name. First, it made a particular form of poverty into a gospel, binding the conscience to an absolute renunciation Scripture nowhere commands and turning a counsel into a law. Second, and gravely, the radical wing embraced Joachim’s scheme of three ages of history—the age of the Father, the Son, and a coming age of the Spirit—a false prophecy that set a new revelation above the closed canon and was rightly condemned by the church. The dictionary honors the protest against worldly wealth while answering that the gospel is not poverty and that no prophecy of Scripture is of any private interpretation; the canon is closed, and no third age is coming.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The rigorist Franciscan party insisting on absolute poverty and entangled with Joachite apocalypticism; honored for protesting church wealth, corrected for making poverty a gospel and adding false prophecy.

SPIRITUAL FRANCISCANS, the rigorist wing of the Franciscan order (13th–14th c.).

Insisted on the strictest observance of Francis’s rule of absolute poverty.

Honored for protesting the wealth and worldliness of the church.

Made a particular poverty a gospel, binding the conscience beyond Scripture.

Embraced Joachim of Fiore’s false scheme of a coming age of the Spirit.

📖 Key Scripture

1Ti 6:8 — "And having food and raiment let us be therewith content."

Mat 6:24 — "No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon."

2Pe 1:20 — "Knowing this first, that no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation."

Rev 22:18 — "For I testify unto every man that heareth the words of the prophecy of this book, If any man shall add unto these things, God shall add unto him the plagues that are written in this book:"

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Their protest against church wealth is honored, but they made a particular poverty a gospel and embraced Joachim’s false prophecy of a coming age of the Spirit above the closed canon.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption to name is twofold. First, the binding of an absolute, particular poverty upon the conscience as though it were the gospel, turning a possible counsel into a required law and making the form of one’s holding of goods the measure of one’s holiness—when Scripture commands contentment, not destitution, and warns only against the service of mammon. Second, and far graver, the embrace of Joachim of Fiore’s apocalyptic scheme of three ages, climaxing in a coming age of the Spirit that would supersede the age of the Son—a false prophecy that set new revelation above the closed canon and was condemned by the church.

The principle to recover is contentment under the sufficiency of Christ and the finality of the closed canon. Having food and raiment, the believer is to be content; the gospel is not poverty but Christ. And no prophecy of Scripture is of any private interpretation; God has spoken finally in His Son, and the man who adds to the words of the prophecy invites the plagues written therein. There is no third age to await; the church lives by the Word once delivered.
